The DRI opposed the pleas contending the SC orders were being relied on out of context.
After the hearing, Justice P M Raval stated, “Considering the orders passed by the apex court granting protection to the present applicants, as aforesaid, it would be in the fitness of things if the execution of lookout circular qua the FIR in questions, be suspended till the returnable date, keeping open all the rights, contentions of the parties before the apex court as and when the matters come up for hearing.” The HC has posted a further hearing of the case on June 29.

title: ‘Concerted fraud’: Gujarat HC cancels acquisition of ‘additional land’ for Ahmedabad–Dholera Expressway - The Indian Express
article_text:
‘Concerted fraud’: Gujarat HC cancels acquisition of ‘additional land’ for Ahmedabad–Dholera Expressway
Says land owners and officials of NHAI and Collector office, Ahmedabad, colluded to siphon off public money in a concerted manner, orders high-level inquiries.
A flipped map, a lightning-fast non-agricultural conversion, and a land sale completed in days — what looked like routine paperwork slowly unravelled into a high-stakes land puzzle, one that the Gujarat High Court would later call a “concerted fraud” on public money.
Finding that private landowners and government authorities, including officials of the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), “colluded to siphon off the public money in a concerted manner”, the High Court cancelled the acquisition of ‘additional land’ for the Ahmedabad–Dholera Expressway and directed the Chairman, NHAI, to initiate fresh, high-level inquiries into the conduct of erring officials.
The Division Bench of Chief Justice Sunita Agarwal and Justice D N Ray of the Gujarat High Court were hearing petitions filed by two private purchasers of the contentious lands, who had sought release of NHAI compensation for the ‘additional land’, subsequently acquired by the highway authority as well as a petition filed by the NHAI alleging a coordinated fraud involving landowners and officials.
The case pertains to lands, located in village Bholad of Dholka taluka in Ahmedabad district, measuring 21,314 sq metres across two contiguous plots bearing survey no. 785, owned by Raghavjibhai Devjibhai and Survey No. 786, owned by Karsanbhai Patel, which was acquired by the NHAI for the Ahmedabad-Dholera Expressway via notifications in 2018 and 2020. The NHAI also awarded the compensation to the land owners.
After the acquisition, the original owners applied to the District Inspector of Land Records (DILR) for remeasurement of the land, in which the DILR allegedly “flipped the geographical locations and boundaries of the two plots in the village map”, the court judgment notes. Taking advantage of this, the original owners obtained a non-agricultural (NA) conversion for a purported “remaining” area of the land from the district collector within 12 days and sold it to private petitioners.
The court judgment notes that “an outcome of mala fide exercise conducted on the part of the officers of the NHAI in collusion with the purchasers” was that the NHAI initiated fresh acquisition proceedings for the same land — now labeled as “additional land” at significantly higher NA rates. The private petitioners sought a writ to compel disbursement of this additional compensation, while NHAI eventually challenged the resurvey and NA conversion.
In its 83-page judgment made available on April 24, the High Court states, “This court categorically recorded that the case presents a glaring picture of collusive acts of Collector office and the Project Implementation Unit of the NHAI with the original owners and occupiers… and the subsequent purchasers… and they (NHAI officials) all have colluded to siphon off the public money in a concerted manner which has resulted in issuance of two subsequent notifications by the Central Government on the premise of requirement of acquisition of additional area… which was actually not available on the date of submission of the proposals dated June 23, 2022 and November 9, 2023 by the NHAI.”’
The court also recorded the statement of the advocate appearing for the NHAI, that the authority “had identified its erring officials posted in the Project Implementation Unit, Ahmedabad, at the relevant point of time, who have been found involved in the entire illegal exercise of making the proposals to issue acquisition notifications of the land which was not available.”
The court judgment notes that the additional compensation of Rs 13.91 crore that was to be disbursed for the non-existent “additional land” was deposited by the office of the Special Land Acquisition Officer on November 18, 2024, and the said amount had “not been disbursed to the land holders on account of the disputes brought to the knowledge of the higher officials.”
Recording that the Additional Chief Secretary, Revenue, did not take care to examine the entire original record of the conversion of the land to non-agricultural by the office of the Collector, who had “completed in a hurried manner…within a period of 12 days without verification of the status of the available land…”, the court directed that this judgment be “placed before the Chief Secretary of the State and the Advocate General for their information by the office of the Registrar General of the High Court.”
The judgment, while quashing the NHAI acquisition notifications for the additional areas of both lands as well as the the exercise of resurvey of land and all consequential maps and actions flowing from such resurvey and the February 2022 order of the District Collector, Ahmedabad, in converting the lands for NA use, stated that the order was “illegal and suffering from vice of mala fide exercise of powers”.
Directing that the compensation amount deposited must be returned and the NHAI must obtain possession of 21,314 square meters of land, the judgment states, “The compensation amount deposited with the competent authority/Land Acquisition Officer for the cancelled notifications shall be refunded back to the NHAI immediately… (The orders are) hereby quashed, found to be the result of a fraudulent exercise conducted in collusion with the officers of the NHAI, office of the DILR/Collector, Ahmedabad, and the erstwhile land owners, as also the petitioners herein.”

title: 13 arrested across Gujarat in Rs 631.86cr cyber fraud network linked to 982 cases nationwide - MorungExpress
article_text:
IANS Photo
Gandhinagar, May 23 (IANS): A major coordinated cybercrime investigation in Gujarat has led to the arrest of 13 accused allegedly linked to a cyber fraud network involving transactions worth over Rs 631.86 crore through mule bank accounts, shell companies and multi-state operations, officials said on Saturday.
The action was carried out under ‘Operation Mule Hunt 2.0’ by the Cyber Centre of Excellence following directives from senior police officials amid a rise in cybercrime cases across the country.
Superintendent of Police (SP) Rajdeepsinh Jhala said the operation was launched on the basis of technical analysis and human intelligence inputs and executed simultaneously across Ahmedabad, Surat, Vadodara, Bharuch and Rajkot.
He said four separate FIRs had been registered over the last four days, leading to the arrest of 13 accused.
“The teams acted in a coordinated manner based on technical and human intelligence inputs under supervision, leading to simultaneous arrests across multiple districts,” SP Jhala said.
According to the police, verification of 45 bank accounts linked to the accused through the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal (NCCRP) revealed 982 cyber fraud complaints registered across India, with more than 200 FIRs lodged in different states.
The total fraudulent transactions linked to the network are estimated to be worth more than Rs 631.86 crore.
Police said one group allegedly operated through a structured setup using a firm named ‘Saurath Overseas’, under which mule bank accounts were opened to route illicit funds.
Investigators stated that Madhavji Kotadiya, in coordination with Vimal Jada, allegedly used breached databases sourced from Telegram channels and other online platforms to obtain banking customer IDs and mobile numbers, which were then allegedly used to target victims with fake credit card offers.
“Vimal Jada is accused of contacting victims using social engineering techniques, obtaining OTPs from them and subsequently changing bank account passwords to gain unauthorised access. Once access was secured, the funds were allegedly withdrawn and transferred into mule accounts operated by the network,” SP Jhala told IANS.
A separate syndicate based in Ahmedabad and Surat allegedly used firms including ‘SNB Aqua Shipping Private Limited’, ‘Zeppelin Overseas Shipping Private Limited’ and ‘DKG Creation and Technologies Gujarat’ as fronts to open mule bank accounts.
Police said these entities were used to route cyber fraud proceeds and launder money in exchange for commissions.
During raids, details of multiple bank accounts and official records were recovered.
Another module allegedly operated from Vadodara and Bharuch, where individuals used accounts opened under names such as ‘Air Conditioning Hub’ and ‘Works Global’.
According to the police, these accounts were allegedly used to transfer and circulate cybercrime proceeds in exchange for commission payments.
Officials said preliminary interrogation revealed that members of the network earned commissions ranging from four per cent to eight per cent for facilitating fraudulent transactions.
The accused are believed to include mule account holders, handlers and coordinators involved in transferring funds through multiple layers.
Police further stated that the network was linked to several categories of cybercrime, including online financial fraud, internet banking fraud, UPI scams, investment fraud and deposit-related fraud.
Analysis of NCCRP data revealed that complaints were registered across multiple states, including Gujarat (77), Maharashtra (137), Karnataka (126), Uttar Pradesh (87), Tamil Nadu (83), Telangana (64), Delhi (53), Rajasthan (47), West Bengal (46), Haryana (38), Kerala (37), Andhra Pradesh (24), Bihar (23), Madhya Pradesh (19), Odisha (16), Jammu and Kashmir (12), Jharkhand (12), Punjab (12), Chhattisgarh (10), Assam (8), Goa (7), Himachal Pradesh (6), Uttarakhand (5), Puducherry (3), Meghalaya (2), Arunachal Pradesh (1), Tripura (1) and Sikkim (1), taking the total number of complaints nationwide to 982.
Among those arrested from Ahmedabad and Surat were Manish Lodha (39), Ankit Lodha (28), Naveen Vaishnav, Mohit Nahar, Madhavji Kotadiya, Nayan Italia, Nimesh Jetani and Vimal Jada.
From Vadodara and Bharuch, Arbaz Pirzada, Faizan Sodagar, Kasifali Sheikh and Mohammad Memon were arrested, while Hardik Sarvaiya was arrested from Rajkot.
Police said the seized material included 28 mobile phones, 39 cheque books linked to different bank accounts, one passbook, two laptops, 12 ATM/debit cards and four stamps belonging to multiple firms, including SNB Aqua Shipping Private Limited, Zeppelin Overseas Shipping Private Limited and DKG Creation and Technologies.
SP Jhala noted that the investigation had revealed a structured cybercrime ecosystem operating through fake firms and mule accounts to conceal illegal proceeds.
“Further investigation is underway to trace the flow of funds and identify remaining associates involved in the network,” he added.
Authorities reiterated that citizens should never share bank account details or OTPs with anyone.

Several kilograms of gold and silver, worth over Rs 4 crore, were seized by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) from Gujarat's Mehsana district in connection with a stock market investment fraud, an official said on Thursday.
Several kilograms of gold and silver, worth over Rs 4 crore, were seized by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) from Gujarat's Mehsana district in connection with a stock market investment fraud, an official said on Thursday.
The ED, Ahmedabad Zonal Office, has recovered and seized silver bullion weighing 110 kg valuing Rs 2.4 crore; gold bullion weighing around 1.296 kg valuing Rs 1.7 crore, silver jewellery weighing 39.7 kg (approximately); Indian currency equivalent to Rs 38.8 lakh; foreign currencies equivalent to at least Rs 10.6 lakh and various property documents in the case of Himanshu alias Pintu Bhavsar and others, said an official in a statement.
The ED made the seizure in "fraudulent stock market investment fraud with common investors" under the provisions of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, said the statement.
The ED initiated investigation on the basis of FIR registered by Kheralu Police station, district Mehsana, under various sections of Indian Penal Code, 1860 against Himanshu alias Pintu Bhavshar and others.
As per the FIR, the accused lured the complainant to invest money in the stock market to earn huge amount of profit and later, defrauded the complainant by not returning his investments.
The accused didn't invest the money of the complainant in any of the shares of any company and used it for personal gains. Later, during the investigation, it came to light that at least six more FIRs were registered by police in different states of India involving total fraud amount to the tune of Rs 10.87 crore.
It was revealed that mastermind Bhavsar along with other accused people opened a number of offices in Mehsana, Visnagar and Vadnagar for the purpose of alluring and getting funds from the common public in the name of investments in the stock market, the ED said.
They hired a number of employees to make regular phone calls to potential investors for obtaining funds for alleged investment in the stock market by luring them with higher returns.
During the investigation under the PMLA, it came to light that Himanshu Bharatkumar Bhavsar used Investment Advisor Certificate issued by SEBI in his individual capacity for the use of Vishwas Stocks Research Pvt. Ltd., Dalal Stocks Advisory Pvt. Ltd. and Devki Stocks Pvt. Ltd for their unregistered investment advisory activities, the ED said.
The three entities did not have any certificate of registration from SEBI to act as investment advisors and to fulfil this requirement tied up with Bhavsar.
The SEBI in its order, held Vishwas Stocks Research Pvt. Ltd., Dalal Stocks Advisory Pvt. Ltd. and Devki Stocks Pvt. Ltd and its Directors namely Himanshu Bharatkumar Bhavsar alias Pintu Bhavsar and others; responsible for violations/contravention committed by offering investment advisory.

The Cybercrime Cell of the Rajkot Rural Police on Wednesday said it has arrested three more persons involved in a racket of creating mule bank accounts and transacting hundreds of crores of rupees in proceeds of crime obtained through cyber frauds in order to hide their trail.
While Manish Kamani, Jay Nadpara, Rushit Rayani, Pravinsinh Parmar, Mahendrasinh Jadeja and Mayursinh Vaghela were arrested on February 13, the three more arrested on February 21 included Adiluddin Mohammed S/O Muniruddin Mohammed of Telangana, Mihir Ramji Rangani and Hiren Ashwin Limbasiya, both of Rajkot. Another accused Lalo alias Yagnik Zalavadiya is yet to be arrested.
SP Vijay Singh Gurjar on Wednesday said that while Rs 23.14 crore worth of fraud amount had been reported as having been deposited in accounts operated by this gang by way of complainants from various states on the Samanvay and NCCRP portals, the fraud amount transacted through the accounts involving the 10 accused in this case is as high as Rs 1,500 crore.
While checking for suspicious mule accounts on the Samanvaya Portal and NCCRP, the Rajkot Rural Police found an account in Yes Bank branch in Moviya, Paddhari, in the name of a firm M/s Jyot Trading Company, in which transactions to the tune of Rs 200 crore had been found. Based on the investigation into these improbable numbers, six persons were booked in an FIR registered at Paddhari Police Station under BNS sections Sections 317(2), 317(5), 318(4), 61(2), 54, and sections 66(d) of the Information Technology Act. The six were subsequently arrested and are currently in judicial custody.
When the police delved into the case, they found several bank accounts in the names of the arrested accused being operated through shell firms including those opened at Agricultural Produce Market Committees (APMCs).

SP Gurjar said that the amounts transacted through these accounts had mainly come from cybercrime, gaming fraud and GST fraud.

title: December discounts: ‘Tis season to be merry for e-crooks in Gujarat - The Times of India
article_text:
Ahmedabad: Last week, a senior Ahmedabad doctor became the latest victim of a fast, precise phishing trap that looked completely legitimate. While trying to buy his annual FASTag pass for frequent Udaipur trips, he searched "Fast Tag Annual Pass" on Google instead of opening the official Rajmarg Yatra app.
A seemingly official link displayed a QR code labelled "FastTag Annual Pass Tag." He paid Rs 3,000, only to realize the next day that the payment had been in vain because the annual pass can be issued only through the govt app. That mistake is exactly what phishing operators are counting on this Dec.
CloudSEK, a cybersecurity firm, has mapped more than 2,000 fake holiday-themed online stores, most activated specifically for Black Friday, Christmas, and New Year discount periods.
CloudSEK's security researcher Ibrahim Saify, who investigated these campaigns, says the scams are "highly polished and designed to exploit rushed decisions and high-volume holiday shopping."
The scammers work with identical phishing kits, shared infrastructure, and psychological pressure — all timed for the season when people buy the fastest and think the slowest. Saify broke down how the scams work. "Fake e-shopping platform brand look-alikes (typosquatting)," his report said.
"Scammers register domains that look extremely close to real brands using tiny spelling differences."
CloudSEK's analysis identified more than 750 interconnected fake sites, including amaboxhub.com; amznbigsale.com; and amazonreturnsbox.com "They are mass-produced storefronts filled with flashy discounts," said the CloudSEK report. Instead of processing payments directly, many phishing sites route transactions through temporary, unflagged "merchant" domains like "georgmat.com" and "thewonsel.com." These shell sites act as intermediaries to evade detection by banking security systems.
The next set of phishing domains falls in the ".shop" brand impersonation network. "Attackers create fake brand stores using the ".shop" extension, including Samsungsafe.shop; Appleipadus.shop; Raybansafe.shop; and Logitechsafe.shop, " the report said.
Many of these stayed in "Coming Soon" mode until days before the sales, switching to active scams just in time for peak shopping traffic.

title: Pay and pass 10th and 12th with guarantee: No school or tuition needed, open schooling racket in Gujarat ex... - Bhaskar English
article_text:
- English News
- Local
- Gujarat
- Ahmedabad
- Gujarat Open Schooling Racket Exposed | 10th & 12th Exam Scam
InvestigationPay and pass 10th and 12th with guarantee:No school or tuition needed, open schooling racket in Gujarat exposed on hidden camera
- Copy link
A gang claiming to help students pass Class 10 and 12 exams by taking money has been exposed. The people involved openly promise to write answers worth 80 to 90 marks during the exam. They tell students not to worry about flying squads, saying their staff is already present inside the exam centres.
They claim there is no need to attend school, tuition classes or complete homework throughout the year. Students are told they can choose any exam centre in Gujarat, simply appear for the exam and get a ‘pass’ result within 45 days. According to them, scoring 45 marks is enough to clear the exam, and they guarantee this for a fixed amount of money.
Board exams usually bring pressure, not only on students but also on the parents. A full year of school, extra classes and long hours of study at home are normally required to score good marks.
However, an investigation has revealed that some people are running such illegal ‘setting’ operations. Hidden camera footage has exposed how they are playing with the future of students and damaging the education system.
Divya Bhaskar's investigation team received information that centers have opened in various cities of Gujarat under the name of 'open schooling' which guarantee passing the 10th and 12th standard examinations. Therefore, we conducted a sting operation on the people running such centers.
First, understand what the concept of open schooling is. Under the Ministry of Education, Government of India, comes NIOS, which stands for National Institute of Open Schooling. It organizes examinations for 10th and 12th standards. If you take the examination through NIOS, its qualification is considered equivalent to that of the Gujarat Education Board and CBSE. That is why, after passing this examination, you can gain admission to any school or college in the country.
Why do people take exams in NIOS instead of the board? The objective of NIOS is to organize exams for people who do not want to attend regular school or for those whose education has been interrupted for some reason. For example, if someone has not completed primary education, they can directly take the 10th standard exam even at an older age without attending school. If someone has dropped out after 10th standard, the 12th standard exam can also be taken through NIOS.
The National Institute of Open Schooling generally organizes exams three times a year. These exams are held approximately one month after the completion of the Gujarat Board exams, i.e., in April-May and October-November. Additionally, once a year, an On-Demand examination is also organized based on the number of candidates.
The main office of NIOS in Gujarat is located in Gandhinagar, and it also has centers in various cities across the state. According to information obtained from the official NIOS website, there are a total of 410 centers in 32 districts of Gujarat. Among these, Vadodara has the highest number of centers with 31, and Ahmedabad has 25 centers. Additionally, there are many centers in Surat, Rajkot, and Anand. However, many of these centers, which started under the guise of educational good deeds, have become epicenters for printing money and irregularities.
According to NIOS rules, a fee of 1800 rupees is charged for male candidates appearing for the 10th standard examination, and 1450 rupees for female candidates. However, when the Divya Bhaskar team visited centers in Vadodara and Ahmedabad, a shocking revelation came to light.
This investigation began with an advertisement found on social media. It readLast chance to get admission in NIOS. An examination will be organized for any student who has failed in standard 10-12. Save your precious year. Along with this, a mobile number was also provided. And a guarantee of passing was also given.
First talk on mobile and then in-person meeting We called the mobile number and had a conversation with a woman. At that time, we identified ourselves as the elder brother of a student. During the telephonic conversation, information such as "When will the exam be held?" and "What documents will be needed?" was provided. But during the inquiry, when we asked about the exam fee, a new chapter was revealed. For male candidates, the fee is 1800 rupees, but we were told that 12,500 rupees would have to be paid.
Explaining the reason behind charging such an exorbitant fee, the woman on the phone claimed to arrange "setting" for the student in the exam and guarantee passing. At the end of the phone conversation, the woman sent us the address and asked us to come meet her in person. Additionally, she also sent us the location on mobile.
When Divya Bhaskar's investigation team reached the Vadodara center We reached the NIOS center located in Vadodara. This center was situated on the third floor of the complex. Outside, there were attractive boards with NIOS written on them.
As soon as we opened the glass door, there was a reception desk where a young woman was sitting. We introduced ourselves as the student's brother and stated that we had come to inquire about the exam.
We also mentioned that we had spoken on the phone earlier. So, after noting down the name and mobile number in the laptop, we were asked to wait for a while.
After telling us to wait, the young woman sitting at the reception went into an office built inside the NIOS center, talking on her mobile phone. In less than a minute, she came out and asked us to meet a madam sitting inside the office. We entered the office.
A young woman was sitting at a table and chair. But there was no computer, laptop, or any other large equipment on the table. Only a few papers were lying there. Our conversation began. The young woman introduced herself as Shraddha Madam.
Read excerpts from the conversation between Divya Bhaskar's reporter and the center manager
Shraddha: Tell me, what happened? Reporter: I want my younger brother to take the 10th standard exam.
Shraddha: Where are you from? Reporter: I am from Waghodia.
Shraddha: What is he doing currently? Reporter: He's not doing anything. He failed 10th standard twice. In 4-4 subjects.
Shraddha: No problem, if he has given exams for all subjects from here, it will be possible, and if the result is after 2021, then doing 4 subjects will also be possible.
Reporter: We want to take exams for all subjects. Shraddha: Okay, that can be done, but there's a fee here. The thing is, they have to go to take the exam. We don't have to do any preparation. But they will have to write as much as we provide. For example, there will be practicals for 3 subjects. They will have to go to school to give the practicals. We will send it in advance. So, they just have to write it and go prepared.
Reporter: So, you will give the papers in advance? Shraddha: Yes... we will send the PDF. They have to write it and keep it ready. According to the hall ticket they provide, they also have to submit books there and take an exam for half to three-quarters of an hour.
Reporter: So, you have to go there and write? Shraddha: Yes... It will be a half-hour exam. So, you will have to write about two pages of answers in it. Our support will be there too, so there won't be any problem. But you will have to go to take the exam compulsorily. Then there will be a theory exam. Our staff will be available there, the answer sheet will arrive on their table. You just have to look and write. If you want to pass with our support in this way, the fee is 22 thousand rupees and 500 rupees will be for admission fees. You will have to make payments in installments. In that, you can first pay 10 thousand, then 5 thousand, and then 7 thousand.
Reporter: We can make the full payment at once. Shraddha: Then the fee will be 20 thousand and 500 rupees will be for form registration.
Reporter: Is there a guarantee of passing in this? Shraddha: There is no guarantee of passing, but there is a guarantee that you will get to write there. They will get plenty to write there. From the center located in Vadodara, we came to know how irregularities occur in the NIOS examination. But the answers to two major questions were still to be found.
- We wanted to know if such malpractice runs in a single center or city, or if a similar network is spread across different cities as well?
- If one wants to take an on-demand exam, what kind of arrangement is made for it?
In search of answers to these questions, we found the address of a center in Ahmedabad. Where agents, sitting without any fear or shame, were openly claiming how they have turned education into a business.
In a complex built on the ring road in Ahmedabad's Odhav area, there is a center of the National Institute of Open Schooling. How does the entire network operate? To expose it, a sting operation was conducted. For this, we reached the NIOS center in Ahmedabad's Odhav area.
This center is operating in a complex where many spa centers operate in the building. We reached the third floor of the four-story building.
On one side, an NIOS board, next to it a spa board, and right beside it, a garbage bin overflowing with filth. Moving a little further, a large glass door appeared, on which information about exams conducted by NIOS was attractively written. It also claimed to provide guidance at this center.
Upon entering, we saw a young woman sitting at the reception to provide initial information to visitors. We approached the young woman, introduced ourselves as the student's brother, and stated the reason for coming to the center. After taking some details, she asked us to sit on the sofa for a while. Even before we arrived, two to three students had come for inquiries.
After waiting for about three minutes, the girl sitting at the reception told us to go to office number one. Another girl was sitting in this office. There was no laptop, computer or any other literature or material on the table. She just had a mobile phone in her hand. The girl introduced herself as 'Saloni Ma'am'.
As soon as we entered the office, the Q&A started even before sitting on the chair.
Saloni, Center Administrator: Who needs to take the exam? Reporter: My brother.
Saloni, Center Administrator: Which standard exam needs to be taken? Reporter: 10th standard.
Saloni, Center Director: Has he failed? Reporter: Yes, last year he failed in 4 subjects in 10th standard.
Saloni, Center Director: We have the NIOS board. If you fill the form from Vadodara, your exam center will also be in Vadodara. We will provide the answer key for writing. We will provide for 80 to 90 marks. We guarantee to provide the answer key. But the student has to write it. If they write quickly, they will definitely pass.
Reporter: How many marks are needed to pass? Saloni, Center Director: 45 marks in this.
Reporter: So many? In the Gujarat Board, 33 marks are passing marks. Saloni, Center Manager: Yes in some, 33 and in some, 35 marks are passing marks. Even in this, one might pass with 35 marks, but 45 are definitely achievable.
Reporter: Where will one have to go to take the exam? Saloni, Center Manager: Its center will be Nadiad. We also provide Nadiad. There is no exam center in Ahmedabad, so the student will have to go to Nadiad. We will provide for 80 to 90 marks, the student will have to write by looking. If they write, they will definitely pass. Then if a student fails and says, "What are you taking money for?" We take money for providing the answer key, for setting it up.
Reporter: What if someone gets caught during checking, if a squad comes? Saloni, Center Manager: They do come. But our staff is always there to help. We will provide the answer key to write from and also give two hours. The student will just have to write quickly and neatly.
Saloni told us, before the exam, you will be given the hall ticket and ID card from here. You will have to print it out and take it to the exam center. The online result will be available 45 days after the exam, and then you will also receive a hard copy.
Thus, the administrator, as if taking pride in the malpractices prevalent in the exam, gave us a lot of information. Yet, some of our questions remained. After some general conversation, we asked for more information to find out the extent to which this scam operates.
Reporter: When will the exam be held? Saloni, Center Administrator: It will be in September-October.
Reporter: After passing, if one wants to study 11th standard regularly, can they? Saloni, Center Administrator: Yes.. but not this year, next year. Since the exam will be in October, they can study 11th in 2027.
Reporter: What is the fee? Saloni, Center Administrator: If you want to take admission now, the fee is 12 thousand 500 rupees.
Reporter: And the writing arrangement? Saloni, Center Operator: All that is included in this.
Reporter: Is this fee for one paper or for all subjects' exams? Saloni, Center Operator: There will be five papers, and you will have to go there for all five days. If you pay all at once, it's 12,500, and if you want to do EMI, it's 15,500. The first installment for that is five and a half thousand.
Reporter: Why is the exam as late as October? It's usually held in April-May, isn't it? I saw it online? Saloni, Center Operator: It comes in February-March. It's called an On-Demand Exam.
Reporter: Can't forms be filled for that? Saloni, Center Operator: The fee for one subject in that is 15,000 rupees, and its forms have also closed.
Reporter: So nothing can be done about it? Saloni, Center Operator: If you want to take the exam, I can arrange to open the link, but for that, you will have to pay 15,000 rupees per subject.
Reporter: Can't anything be done reasonably? Saloni, Center Operator: No sir nothing can be done about that. The 12,500 rupees fee is already low right now. Otherwise, last year the fee was 17,500.
Saloni had asked us to send the student's documents via WhatsApp. So, pretending that we would provide the documents shortly, we left from there.
First in Vadodara and then in Ahmedabad, it became clear in the sting operations of both centers that large-scale irregularities are going on in the name of NIOS examinations, and thousands of rupees are being extorted from students indiscriminately.

title: Rising marriage fraud among Gujarat NRIs fuels pre-wedding investigation trend: Matrimonial detectives reve... - Bhaskar English
article_text:
- English News
- Local
- Gujarat
- Ahmedabad
- Rising Marriage Fraud With Gujaratis NRI Increase Pre wedding Investigation Trend: Probing Fiancée And Family Background; Bhaskar Talks With Matrimonial Detectives To Understand Scam
Rising marriage fraud among Gujarat NRIs fuels pre-wedding investigation trend:Matrimonial detectives reveal scams as families & fiancées’ backgrounds are scrutinised
- Copy link
The Diwali festivals are over. Wedding season will arrive in a short time. Parents' biggest worry is what kind of match their child will get? This worry becomes more intense when it comes to foreign countries.
When a boy or girl lives abroad, people take the route of getting them investigated. Getting investigations done before arranging marriages abroad is not new. This has been going on for a long time but some cases have come to light that are shocking.
First read such cases....
Case 1 A boy living in Canada was going to get engaged to a girl living in Ahmedabad, but due to some suspicion, the boy contacted a detective agency and asked for an investigation. During this investigation, it was discovered that the people the girl had shown as her parents were actually not her parents at all.
The name the girl gave for her brother and the name that came up in the investigation were different. Not just this, but the address given by the girl was also a very common address.
When the detectives reached that address for investigation, an elderly couple lived there. The names the girl had shown as her parents were the names of this couple. It was also discovered that the girl with whom marriage talks were going on was already married. After this, the detectives obtained the girl's address and investigated it, finding that the girl was very happy in her married life.
In this case, it was discovered that some people were committing fraud using the girl's name. The scammers had extracted details through the internet. The NRI boy was being trapped in this way. The boy had already given gifts worth more than 10 lakhs rupees.
Case 2 This case is not from Gujarat but it had shocked even the detectives.
A father and his elder son went for the investigation of the younger brother because the family was showing many girls to the younger brother but he wasn't liking any girl. Every time after seeing a girl, he would refuse saying that he doesn't want to marry that girl. After this, the detective agency arranged a session with the boy.
During the session, it was observed that the boy is attracted to and looks at beautiful girls and women passing by. Meanwhile, the detectives noted some things and left. After that, they spoke with his father and informed him that while his son is attracted to females, it is shocking that he is not getting married.
After this, surveillance was conducted for a week. It was noticed that the boy went to the same hotel three to four times in a week. During this time, there was also a beautiful girl with him. Each time, the same girl was seen with him.
The agency felt that this girl must be having an affair with him. After completing the surveillance, we called his father and his elder son also came along. The agency showed them the girl's photo and said that your younger son is involved with this girl.
Upon seeing the photo, the father and his elder son went quiet and gave no response. The boy's father said that this is my elder son's wife. Thus it was revealed that the younger brother-in-law was having an affair with his sister-in-law.
Case 3
A family came to Gujarat from America and arranged their son's marriage with a girl. After that, they had a court marriage, completed the process of joint bank accounts and returned to America. After which they worked on the documentation of visa file for the wife. During this process, a period of 3 to 4 months had passed.
Meanwhile, the girl reduced communication with that boy. When the boy started asking her everything, the girl was giving roundabout answers, so the boy became suspicious and contacted for investigation. When inquiring about the girl, it was revealed that the girl had affairs. Photos and videos were collected as evidence and given to that boy. During client counseling, it was discovered that the girl had married due to pressure from her parents.
Case 4
Before getting engaged, a boy living in Canada told the girl's family that he owns a petrol pump. When they investigated about him
An inquiry came for a boy living in Canada. It was to find out about his character and whether what he said was true or not. After we started investigating about that boy, we found out that he had claimed to be the owner of a petrol pump but in reality there was nothing like that.
He used to drink a lot of alcohol. When the girl with whom his marriage was fixed went to visit Canada, instead of keeping her at home, the boy kept her in a hotel.
According to detective agencies, now more inquiries come for investigating girls. Generally, inquiries come for investigating boys and girls between 21 to 35 years of age.
What kind of investigations do young men and women living abroad conduct about their partners when they come to Gujarat for marriage? Which country's NRIs conduct the most pre-marriage investigations? What kinds of doubts do they have about their partners before and after marriage? What challenges arise when investigating someone living abroad? What kinds of lies do NRIs tell when they come for marriage?
Bhaskar discussed these and many other questions with Baldev Puri, who started working as a detective in 1986 and is currently the chairman of AMX Detective, and Shiv Shah, owner of The National Detective Service.
Indian or Gujarati is the first choice for marriage
Baldev Puri told Bhaskar, 'While I have been associated with this field for the last 38 years, I have focused more on matrimonial since 2002. This practice has become very popular in the last 10 years.
First in cities like Ahmedabad, Vadodara and gradually its popularity increased across Gujarat. Because for many years now, the craze to settle abroad has been increasing among Indians. In such circumstances, even though they settle abroad, Indian or Gujarati is still the first choice for their son or daughter's marriage in their family.
'Let's say if a person is in Canada or London or in America, before getting married here, they come to us with cases to investigate the girl or boy. After which we verify that person. When Gujarat cases come to us, they investigate what work the NRI boy or girl does there abroad and what their character is like.'
Investigates about girl and family
'We receive many investigation cases from abroad for Gujarat. In these cases, NRI boys get investigations done through us about Gujarati girls and their families. They want to obtain details about whether the girl they are going to marry and her family are suitable or not.
In such circumstances, when we start the investigation, we find out that all of these are scammers. Because in some cases, it has happened that someone pretends to be the girl's parents, while others pretend to be her siblings.'
'This is how they are scamming NRI individuals. I'm not saying that NRIs don't scam - we get those cases too. Out of 10 cases that come to us, 7 cases are scams or turn out to be false. While only about 3 investigation cases are genuine.'
Boys get more investigations done of girls
Baldev Puri further stated that earlier girls used to come to us the most for investigations, but times have changed now. Now boys have started getting investigations done of girls. Because the law, society and whatever other systems exist are with the girls.
I'm not talking about NRIs, I'm talking in general. Earlier girls used to get pre-marriage investigations done but now boys do it. Now the proportion of girls getting post-marriage investigations has increased.
'There is a difference in investigation charges for people living in India and abroad. During investigations, we face more challenges in India while investigations abroad are completed easily. However, in some countries like UAE, investigations cannot be conducted on any person. We receive cases of boys and girls between 21 to 35 years of age. In some instances, we also get shocking cases involving people of older age.'
More cases come from America and Canada
Shiv Shah told Bhaskar that we mostly get cases from NRIs living in America, Canada, London, Australia and UAE when they come to Gujarat for marriage and want to investigate the other party. About 40% of our cases come from America, 40% from Canada, and 10-10% cases come from Australia and UAE.
Currently, the proportion of marriages based on intercaste and online profile selection has increased. Because of this, the number of cases coming to us now has increased by 40 to 50% compared to cases coming 5 years ago.
'When an NRI person selects a profile here, they have many doubts. What is the character of the boy or girl they have chosen? What is their family background? How many years has the family been living there? Does the boy or girl have any medical problems? Have they been married before? Are they divorced? If divorced, what were the reasons? Such inquiries come to us.'
After disputes arise, suspicions between each other increase
'When NRI people come to India or Gujarat, they have very limited time. During these days, they are also looking for a partner for themselves, so they check profiles of some boys or girls. During this, if they like someone's profile, they talk and do court marriage with that boy or girl.
After that, when they return abroad, they start the PR process to take their partner there. Initially everything goes well but if there is any dispute, their suspicions increase and they come to us for inquiry to resolve it.'
Parents don't check the background of potential matches
'When marriage proposals come from abroad, the prospective bride or groom stays here for about ten days. Then they leave. In such circumstances, Gujarati parents of boys and girls think that they have received a proposal from America and Canada and become overjoyed. They don't investigate the background of the boy or girl.'
'In such cases, I want to tell parents that they need to be cautious. Because these people claim they have motel businesses, petrol pumps, businesses there, but when we investigate, none of this exists. We recently investigated a case where the boy had claimed they had a very good financial condition in America, but when we checked, we found out that the boy was just working at a store.'
7 out of 10 cases involve surveillance of girls
'Compared to before, the proportion of investigation cases for girls has increased more than boys. In such circumstances, out of 10 cases that come to us, 7 cases are for girls while 3 cases are for boys. I have been running this agency for the last 14 years.
We also have tie-ups with agencies abroad. So when we get an investigation request for someone abroad, we contact these agencies to get the work done. The kind of deep inquiry that can be done for a person in India cannot be done in the same way abroad.'
Investigation charge in the country is 30 to 35 thousand rupees
'Marriage is a very easy way to get foreign visas. In such circumstances, people who want to commit fraud get married to boys or girls to reach foreign soil. When someone gets an investigation done here, it costs between 30 to 35 thousand rupees according to their basic demands.
When we want to know about someone abroad, we have to process it in 2 ways. First, we have to investigate their family living here, and we also have to investigate the person abroad whom they are going to marry.'
'If a person has 30 or 40% doubt about their partner, they take this kind of service from us for resolution. Some people succeed in this. While some people's doubts are cleared. Most of these cases are seen more among high-profile people.'

title: Gujarat scholarship scam: Rs 4.60 crore embezzled, four arrested - The New Indian Express
article_text:
AHMEDABAD: A massive Rs 4.60 crore scholarship scam has been busted in Junagadh, Gujarat, where 12 educational institutions siphoned off funds meant for Scheduled Caste students by using fake documents.
Police have arrested four key accused, while a manhunt is on for another administrator as the probe deepens.
The scam has rocked Junagadh, exposing a deep-rooted nexus between educational institutions and alleged corruption in welfare schemes. Funds meant to empower Scheduled Caste students were embezzled, leaving thousands of deserving youths cheated of their rights.
The case came to light after Kishore Bharkhada, Deputy Director of the Scheduled Caste Welfare Office, lodged a formal complaint, triggering the formation of a Special Investigation Team (SIT) led by the Deputy Superintendent of Police, Junagadh City Division.
Acting swiftly, investigators seized documents related to 2,245 students submitted by 12 institutions, which became the foundation of the probe.
Upon scrutiny, investigators discovered that between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2016, administrators of these institutions hatched a calculated conspiracy.
They fabricated student records and submitted them as genuine to the welfare office. These fake documents were then used to issue scholarship cheques, which were pocketed by the accused, never reaching the students they were intended for.
The SIT also sought detailed records from banks linked to these institutions. After cross-checking financial transactions, the involvement of five prime accused surfaced.
The Special Operations Group (SOG) of Gujarat Police moved in and arrested four of them, Ramesh Kalubhai Baku, Ramanik Nathabhai Rathod, Bhavin Laljibhai Dadhaniya, and Jagdish Bhikhabhai Parmar.
A manhunt has been launched to nab Umar Farooq Ibrahim Amrelia, Administrator and Principal of Mangrol’s Indian Institute, who remains absconding.
Investigators revealed that the scam involved a staggering ₹4,60,38,550, stolen over a three-year period. The revelation has sent shockwaves through the Scheduled Caste community, where students are now grappling with anger and distrust towards institutions meant to support them.
Junagadh C Division Police have filed cases against the principals, trustees, and other office-bearers of the implicated institutions. Authorities have warned that more arrests could follow as the investigation widens.
This scandal has sparked outrage, raising serious questions about the accountability of educational institutions and the safeguards within Gujarat’s scholarship system.
The betrayal of vulnerable students has now become a flashpoint for public anger, with calls for stricter oversight and swift justice.

title: Gujarat police bust international cyber fraud racket; six held, crores seized - The New Indian Express
article_text:
AHMEDABAD: Gujarat police have cracked open an international cyber fraud racket, arresting six men linked to scams spanning multiple states.
The gang is accused of duping victims through layered money transfers, with police recovering Rs 3.16 crore cash, 15 mobiles, and cheque books.
Investigations so far trace transactions worth a staggering Rs 23.23 crore tied to the racket.
What began as a complaint of a Rs 25,000 fraud by a youth from Ahmedabad’s Paldi Area turned into a massive breakthrough.
Ahmedabad police, while probing bank transactions linked to the case, discovered that the stolen money was being routed through multiple layers of accounts. By the third layer, the money trail led to Union Bank accounts, where suspicious self-check withdrawals were being made.
ACP S.M. Patel of Ahmedabad N Division revealed that police tracked cash withdrawals of Rs 3.18 crore through rented accounts, complete with pre-signed cheque books.
The scheme was simple yet dangerous money laundered across layers, withdrawn in bulk, and kept ready in cash piles.
The shocking stash of notes left police stunned during the raids.
Digging deeper, cops found that one Yes Bank account tied to the fraud already carried 136 cyber complaints on the national coordination portal (NCCRP).
Another account, under the name Jubilee Hills Merchant, was flagged with 518 complaints, connecting the gang to nationwide scams.
In total, fraud transactions worth Rs 23.23 crore have surfaced, with Rs 9.68 crore of illicit disbursements identified.
The six arrested have been named as Arifkhan Akbarkhan Makrani , Ashwinkumar Natwarlal Patel, Smit Satishchandra Chavda, Rakesh Sawram Prajapati, and Jagdishkumar Mahendrabhai Patel. Each played a role in fueling the racket that spanned across states.
From a small fraud complaint to unearthing a Rs 23 crore racket, Gujarat police have exposed how cyber gangs launder money through multi-layered accounts and rented identities, leaving a long trail of cheated victims across India.

title: Ludhiana: Gujarat man booked for duping 25 Punjab youths in ₹4cr visa scam - Hindustan Times
article_text:
Ludhiana: Gujarat man booked for duping 25 Punjab youths in ₹4cr visa scam
The scam came to light after three youths reached abroad with fake work permit, majority of victims are from Ludhiana, say police
The Ludhiana police have booked a Gujarat-based travel consultant for allegedly duping 25 youths from Punjab, most of them from Ludhiana, of nearly ₹4 crore by promising genuine UK work permit visas that later turned out to be fake.
The accused has been identified as Mihul Soni, director of Current Consultant Private Limited, based in Gandhinagar, Gujarat. He has been booked under relevant sections of cheating, criminal breach of trust and provisions of the Immigration Act.
The case was registered at Division Number 5 police station on the complaint of Sukhchain Singh, a resident of Jaiton in Faridkot, who is also a travel agent operating from Ludhiana.
According to police, Singh approached Soni in June 2025 to arrange UK work permits for 25 of his clients, the majority of whom were from Ludhiana.
Police said Soni allegedly assured Singh that he would arrange genuine work permit visas, collected the documents of the youths and received more than ₹4 crore from them in installments. Acting on these assurances, three youths were sent to the UK.
The fraud came to light after the youths reached the UK and discovered that the work permits issued to them were invalid. Facing difficulties and harassment abroad, all three returned to India within a short span and informed the complainant.
Following this, Singh confronted Soni but allegedly received evasive responses. He then approached police officials in Ludhiana, prompting a preliminary inquiry that continued for nearly six months. Based on the findings of the inquiry, police registered an FIR against Soni at Division Number 5 police station.
ASI Sukhdeep Singh, the investigating officer, said, “Efforts are underway to arrest the accused and the investigation is also focused on identifying whether any accomplices were involved and if more youths were duped using a similar modus operandi.”
Police have urged aspirants planning to go abroad for employment to verify the credentials and registration of travel agents and immigration consultants before making payments.

title: Gujarat: Cybercrime busts gang issuing fraud SIM cards to foreign countries; cyberfraud cases up by 200 per cent - WION
article_text:
Cyber fraud cases are increasing significantly across India, and in a recent operation, the Ahmedabad Cyber Crime Unit has arrested three accused for allegedly issuing and circulating fraudulently activated SIM cards and then selling them to international cybercrime syndicates.
The arrested individuals – Vijay Rawal, Shubham Paradiya, and Kiran Thakkar – allegedly misused customer documents to activate multiple SIM cards and sent them overseas through local agents. These SIM cards were used by call centres engaged in cyber scams targeting Indian citizens.
“During our investigation, we found that SIM cards were routed to Dubai, Cambodia, and Myanmar, where large-scale cyber fraud operations are allegedly run by Chinese networks,” said an official. To figure out how the scam came to light, police began investigating after a Chandlodia resident was defrauded using a SIM card obtained without his knowledge.
The accused Raval had taken his documents under the pretext of transferring an existing number, but instead used them to issue a new SIM card. According to the details, the accused Raval ran a makeshift SIM-issuing centre and fraudulently got the victim’s documents. Raval then claimed that the server was down and assured the victim that the SIM would get auto-activated.
He used the documents to get an Airtel SIM, which later helped in a digital arrest scam. It was also used in operations that lured youth to Southeast Asian countries and trapped them in cyber-slavery. Raval led cops to Pradia, who revealed he bought pre-activated SIM cards from Raval for Rs 700 each and sold them to Thakkar, who sold them to the gang members for Rs 1200 each.
Now, officials are investigating how these SIM cards reached the Southeast Asia-based gangs. Officials say cyber fraud is increasing significantly in Gujarat, with a substantial rise in complaints, financial losses, and sophisticated tactics used by criminals. The state has seen a 200 per cent increase in complaints compared to previous years, with over Rs 1,011 crore lost in the first nine months of 2025.

Gujarat GST uncovers massive ₹560 crore bogus billing scam:CA Alkesh Pedhadiya under investigation for tax evasion, fake ITC misuse and financial manipulation

The Gujarat State GST (SGST) Department has uncovered a massive scam involving ₹560 crore in bogus billing and ₹112 crore in tax evasion, centred on Jamnagar-based Chartered Accountant Alkesh Pedhadiya. A police complaint has been filed, and officials anticipate further shocking revelations as the investigation progresses.
Based on intelligence and prior investigation, the SGST department conducted simultaneous raids on 25 locations in Jamnagar on October 3. This included Pedhadiya’s office, ‘Brahm Associates,’ and his residence. The operation involved 27 teams from GST offices across the state and was conducted under the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017.
Misuse of GST numbers and fake invoices
Investigations revealed 14 bogus companies creating false invoices and claiming Input Tax Credit (ITC) without the actual supply of goods. Pedhadiya allegedly misused the GST numbers of genuine taxpayers, leaving them shocked. Many victims have stated they may file FIRs for fraud and breach of trust.
Evidence seized during raids
Documents, computers, and digital devices were seized from Pedhadiya’s office, uncovering false billing, financial manipulation, and evidence of money laundering. Investigators also discovered hawala transactions through multiple bank accounts. Several companies under scrutiny have accepted the department’s findings and agreed to pay taxes with interest and penalties.
Freezing of bank accounts and asset seizure
The SGST Department blocked fake ITC worth ₹4.62 crore, froze bank accounts holding over ₹1 crore, and provisionally attached movable and immovable assets worth ₹36 crore. Additionally, some taxpayers voluntarily agreed to pay around ₹33 crore in tax, interest, and penalties.
Legal action and enforcement
The SGST Department reaffirmed its zero-tolerance policy against GST fraud. Strict legal action, including penalties, property confiscation, and prosecution, will be taken against all involved.
Of the 25 taxpayers investigated, 14 have been identified as Non-Genuine Taxpayers (NGTP), and further measures are underway to secure government revenue. Despite multiple summons, Pedhadiya has not appeared, prompting the issuance of a Look Out Circular (LOC) to prevent him from leaving the country. Authorities are intensifying efforts to ensure his appearance.
Key findings
- Bogus Transactions: ₹560 crore with ₹112 crore tax evasion.
- ITC Blocked: ₹4.62 crore blocked; bank accounts over ₹1 crore frozen.
- Asset Seizure: Movable and immovable assets worth ₹36 crore provisionally attached.
- Tax Collection: Taxpayers agreed to pay ₹33 crore in taxes, penalties, and interest.
- Legal Proceedings: Investigation ongoing, strict action planned against all involved parties.
The investigation continues, with authorities determined to recover government revenue and penalise those responsible.

title: Phishing emails, threatening calls: Gujarati duo cheats 25 Americans of $2.7 million; 1 sentenced to 63 m - The Times of India

AHMEDABAD: Two young men from Gujarat, living in the United States on student visas, ran a month-long scam and cheated 25 elderly Americans out of nearly $2.7 million.
According to police sources, they used fear and well-planned deception to target the victims in 2024. The sentence was announced on Wednesday by a federal court in Austin.
Kishan Patel, 20, from Navsari, was sentenced to 63 months in a US federal prison for conspiracy to commit money laundering. His co-accused, Dhruv Mangukiya, 21, pleaded guilty and is awaiting sentencing.
According to court records, the fraud ran from July to Aug 2024. Patel and Mangukiya, along with other unnamed conspirators, impersonated US govt officials to target vulnerable seniors. Using phishing emails and threatening phone calls, they convinced victims to part with large sums of cash and even gold, claiming the victims faced legal trouble unless they complied.
Patel allegedly acted as the collector. "He visited victims' homes to pick up the money, keeping a portion for himself and routing the rest to others involved. The value of the scam was pegged at $2,694,156," said a source.
The net closed in when Patel was arrested by Granite Shoals Police on Aug 24, 2024, while retrieving a package believed to contain $1,30,000 in cash from a victim's residence. He was handed over to federal authorities five days later and pleaded guilty on March 18. On June 17, US district judge Robert Pitman sentenced him.
"This defendant took advantage of his visa status and preyed on the fears of vulnerable seniors," said US attorney Justin Simmons. "The sentence reflects our commitment to protect victims of such schemes."

title: Hacked 2.0: Hackers prowl corridors of power in Gujarat - The Times of India
article_text:
Gujarat's highest-ranking officials are used to protecting the public. But when Gujarat's top IAS and IPS officers gathered for Hacked 2.0 on Thursday, they were confronted by a stark reality: Not just their machines, but the officers themselves need protection. Cybercriminals and espionage rings consider bureaucrats as direct gateways into govt networks.
With artificial intelligence (AI) making attacks quicker, quieter and more personalised, human oversight becomes the weakest link. For officials handling sensitive national data, even a single lapse could open the door to a silent breach.
The third session of Hacked 2.0 — a joint initiative of The Times of India and the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU) — made it clear that the next phase of cyberwarfare will not require complex intrusion tools. Setting the tone, Prof Naveen Kumar Chaudhary, campus director of NFSU Goa, stressed the urgency of implementing the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 across govt offices. "With the use of AI increasing at all levels of governance, need of the hour is also to train human resources to quickly identify and respond to cybersecurity threats," said Prof Chaudhary.
Prof Nilay Mistry, head of the Centre for Excellence for Digital Forensics, presented one of the most unsettling scenarios: an attack that needs nothing more than a camera.
Demonstrating the next-generation exploit, he described multi-colour QR codes capable of hijacking device data without internet, GPS or any form of connectivity. "No logs created, no ISP, no IP," he said, underscoring how such "air-gap bypassing" attacks leave investigators with almost no digital evidence.
Mistry also warned that for as little as $30 (Rs 2,660 approx), criminals can buy Telegram-based kits that carry out live OTP bypass attacks. Victims receive what sounds like a routine bank IVR call from a foreign number. Pressing ‘0' transfers the OTP to the attacker in real time. Mistry further demonstrated how advanced persistent threats (APT) were deployed by the attackers during Operation Sindoor to target computer networks and critical infrastructure.
The conversation then shifted to deepfakes — now a major threat to public officials whose careers depend heavily on reputation. Mistry highlighted tools capable of generating ‘Deep Nude' images from a single photograph, as well as websites that can transform a real-time video call by swapping the caller's face instantly.
He reminded the audience that prevention through simple digital hygiene — regular password changes, timely backups and installing genuine software updates — remains the strongest defence. "Today's attacks do not wait for human error. AI-driven bots probe systems non-stop until they find a crack, then quietly steal or encrypt data," said Prof Mistry.
Senior cybersecurity expert Dhaval Sampat reinforced that despite the rise of high-tech intrusions, attackers still prefer human manipulation. "Phishing, vishing and spear phishing remain the top attack vectors," he said. He cited Pakistan-based APT 36, whose malicious PDF titled like ‘Minutes of Meeting by the Raksha Mantri' succeed because victims inherently trust the sender. "They open the file, allowing the malware to install and exfiltrate data quietly." Attackers now scrape social media, WhatsApp statuses and personal details to craft messages that feel familiar and safe, he reminded officers.
For Gujarat's top administrators, the takeaway was unmistakable: AI-powered crime has collapsed the distance between hacker and high office.

title: 3 illegal telephone exchanges busted in Gujarat under IB lens - The Times of India
article_text:
AHMEDABAD: An illegal telephone exchange not only causes losses worth crores to the public exchequer but also potentially poses a serious threat to national security as the calls bypass the legal telecommunication network and cannot be traced by security agencies. The busting of three such digital exchanges in Gujarat - two in Ahmedabad and one in Anand - over the past year and a half has drawn the attention of the central Intelligence Bureau (IB).
The investigative agency is now preparing a report on the rackets where international calls made using VoIP (voice over internet protocol) facility are converted into local calls using computer software and equipment like sim boxes, routers, transceivers, and servers.
According to sources in the state police, central agencies, and the department of telecommunications (DoT), these exchanges can be operated from a small room, a car, or even a scooter to make calls for extortion, cyber frauds, or to run an organized crime network.
"As these exchanges threaten national security, the central Intelligence Bureau (IB) along with DoT is preparing a report on such exchanges," said a home department official.
An officer of a central agency said there are high chances that these exchanges were being used for illegal activities like money laundering, phishing scams, and hawala, which can cause significant financial loss or potentially pose a security threat to the country.
A sim box can route international phone calls as local calls. Each sim box can be fitted with hundreds of GSM sim cards. The exchanges convert an international call from a cellphone to VoIP and then process it through a SIM box which converts the VoIP to a local call.
‘Cops could raid illegal exchanges as sim boxes were stationary’The security agencies could bust the digital exchanges in Gujarat as the sim boxes, which had 32 to 264 sim cards, were stationary.
“If the sim box had been in an urban area, it would not have raised suspicion when 100 sim cards were detected operating in one area. However, if too many sim cards are found operating insecluded places, villages, highways or moving from one place to another, it raises doubts,” said a Gujarat police officer.
The officer said the state home department and DoT constantly coordinate to stop the operation of such digital exchanges.
In August 2021, the Anand local crime branch raided Memon Colony in Borsad town of Anand district and arrested two menfor running a digital exchange. Police seized four sim boxes and 64 sim cards during the raid.
In December 2021, the Ahmedabad crime branch busted an illegal digital telephone exchange in the CG Road area and arrested Tabrez Kataria, a Sarkhej resident operating the racket. Kataria was running the exchange at the behest of one Sheriyar from Dhaka in Bangladesh.Nearly 43 lakh calls were made by residents of India,Pakistan and Bangladesh from Saudi Arabia within a month using this exchange. However, the cops could find details of around 2,700 calls only. This digital exchange caused a loss of nearly Rs 100 crore to the public exchequer.
In February 2022, the Gujarat anti-terrorist squad (ATS) raided a commercial complex on S G Road in Bodakdev and arrested three persons: Jay Shah, 32, a resident of Satellite; Hardik Parmar, 25, a resident of New Ranip; and Anwar Abdul Jabbar Sharif, 35, a native of Tamil Nadu. They had taken 150 SIP (session initiation protocol) lines, converting international calls made through the internet to local calls. The exchange was being run under the garb of a customer care centre for a gold firm.

title: How Cyber Slavery Kingpin From Gujarat Was Caught Before Fleeing - Vibes Of India
article_text:
Five FIRs. A network across at least three states. Agents from Pakistan to China. Over 500 victims trapped in cyber slavery. All in less than two years. Gujarat Police say this is the work of 29-year-old Nilesh Purohit, also called Neel or ‘The Ghost’.
Startling details have emerged in a detailed investigative report by a national daily.
The police caught him more than 20 days ago, the report reveals. They are still unraveling his operations.
The arrest almost failed. On November 16, a Gujarat Police team was traveling from Gandhinagar to Anand, about 100 km, when they got a tip. Purohit was in Ahmedabad.
The Airport police were warned not to let him board a flight. He was reportedly heading to Malaysia. The team reached the international terminal in time and arrested him. The police said, had they been a few minutes late, ‘The Ghost’ would have vanished again.
Purohit was sent to police remand in two cases. He is now in judicial custody at Sabarmati Central Jail.
He faces five FIRs, including human trafficking. Two FIRs are by the Gandhinagar Cyber Centre of Excellence. One by Surat City Police. One each by cyber cells in Maharashtra and West Bengal.
The CBI is also investigating him in at least two international cyber slavery cases. A day before his arrest, he allegedly sent a youth from Punjab to Cambodia.
The Cyber Centre of Excellence said Purohit sent over 500 citizens to cyber slavery. Countries included India, Sri Lanka, Philippines, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Nigeria, Egypt, Cameroon, Benin, and Tunisia. Destinations were Myanmar, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Thailand, sometimes via Dubai.
The report details his past. Purohit is from Anand. His parents ran a catering business. He left studies after Class 12. He did not continue the family catering business. He tried a finance business, but it failed.
Early 2024, he went to Dubai. He got a job through an agent at Dubai Investment Park. The firm was allegedly involved in cybercrime.
He met Pakistani and Chinese agents there. They introduced him to global cyber slavery operations.
He wanted firsthand experience. He travelled to Thailand, then illegally entered Myanmar, and visited cyber fraud sites.
One of the sites was KK Park in Myanmar. It was run by a Chinese gang. The Myanmar army recently raided it. Many employees forced to work there escaped. The largest chunk were allegedly Indians.
In the last three years, India, with help from Thailand and Myanmar, brought back 4,000 citizens from camps like KK Park.
In the middle of last year, Purohit tested the route commonly used by traffickers. He flew to Bangkok, drove 450 km north to Tak City, hiked 15–20 km through the jungle, took a boat on the Moei or Thaungyin river, crossed into Myanmar, and hiked a short distance to KK Park in Myawaddy Township.
He stayed for a month at KK Park, learning operations. Inspector Manali Radadiya said he was successful almost immediately due to good relations with other agents.
He earned Rs 1.76–3.96 lakh per cyber slave. After paying 30–40% to sub-agents, he still earned well. Police believe he trafficked his first person from Gujarat to Myanmar in October 2024.
He used mule accounts and more than five Binance crypto wallets to manage money.
Once trapped, victims could not leave easily. At KK Park, they were forced to sign two-year contracts. Those who wanted out early had to pay Rs 3.5–5 lakh.
Purohit ran a base in Bangkok. He arranged tickets and logistics with Chinese agents.
The Cyber Centre of Excellence said he managed 126 sub-agents. They contacted more than 30 Pakistani agents. The network included over 100 Chinese and foreign companies.
He reached victims through WhatsApp, Telegram, Facebook, and Instagram. Promised jobs, often data entry. Word-of-mouth helped the network grow.
At least 22 youths from Gujarat were directly trafficked. Others came from different states and abroad. Police are confirming names one by one.
Gujarat Police arrested six of his sub-agents in state cases.
Victims realised something was wrong only after reaching Bangkok. Passports were taken. They were driven to KK Park by armed agents.
Furthermore, they were forced into phishing, crypto scams, Ponzi schemes, and dating app fraud. Those who resisted faced physical and mental harassment. Many were too traumatized to file FIRs, so the state filed complaints on their behalf.
Purohit hid online as ‘Ghost’. Sub-agents eventually exposed him. Police arrested him before he could flee India.
Tips came from multiple sources. On November 5, Hitesh Arjan Somaiya of Porbandar was arrested for trafficking 12 youths. On November 13, Sonal Faldu was arrested based on victim statements.
Both sub-agents named Purohit as their superior. Victims also confirmed him. He had provided tickets to Thailand.
Gujarat Police are coordinating with other states that have cases against him.

title: Mastermind Behind Cyber-Slavery Network Arrested in Gujarat - Vibes Of India

The Gujarat Cyber Centre of Excellence (CCoE) has busted an international human trafficking and cyber-slavery ring, apprehending its alleged leader, Nilesh Purohit, also known as Neel or “The Ghost.”
Alongside him, five associates—including a married couple—have been taken into custody. The syndicate, which operated out of Southeast Asian nations, specifically targeted Indian citizens, including numerous individuals from Gujarat, by luring them with fake employment opportunities.
Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghvi, who oversees the Home Department, told reporters that investigations revealed Purohit managed a global network comprising over 126 sub-agents. “He maintained connections with agents in Pakistan and collaborated with around 100 companies across various countries that supplied manpower to cyber-fraud centers in Southeast Asia,” Sanghvi said.
Purohit was apprehended in Gandhinagar while attempting to flee the country. His associates arrested include Hitesh Somaiya, Sonal Phaldu, Bhavdeep Jadeja, and Hardeep Jadeja, along with Sonal’s husband, Sanjay.
The Deputy Chief Minister highlighted that Purohit was linked to the trafficking of more than 500 individuals from countries such as India, Sri Lanka, the Philippines, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Nigeria, Egypt, Cameroon, Benin, and Tunisia to nations including Myanmar, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Thailand. Victims were deceived through social media ads promising high-paying overseas data-entry jobs.
“After confiscating their passports, the accused transported the victims across borders into Myanmar via routes near KK Park and Myawaddy Township. Once there, they were compelled to engage in illegal online operations, including phishing, cryptocurrency scams, Ponzi schemes, and fraudulent dating apps,” he further said.
Records suggest Purohit earned between $2,000 and $4,500 per victim, distributing 30% to 40% of the amount to his sub-agents. “The financial flow was managed through multiple bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets,” the Deputy Chief Minister noted.
He also said that the Government of India, in coordination with authorities in Thailand and Myanmar, executed joint operations that rescued nearly 4,000 individuals. “Many of the rescued persons identified Purohit as the coordinator who had sent them abroad. A case was registered, and an in-depth investigation was launched,” he said.
Officials explained that the CCoE had been continuously analyzing data, including interviews of returnees shared by central agencies such as the I4C, and tracking suspicious activities of agents linked to these scam centers. “Specialized teams were formed for technical assessments, digital forensics, interrogations, and field operations. Intelligence collected through these efforts helped identify agents involved in trafficking victims to cyber-fraud hubs across Southeast Asia,” they said.
Detailing the syndicate’s modus operandi, officials said the perpetrators reached out to citizens through social media or peer referrals, offering lucrative jobs abroad. Once a target expressed interest, the agents conducted interviews and arranged travel and other logistics, often instructing the victims to enter on tourist visas.
“Upon arrival at Bangkok airport, victims were received by armed Malaysian or Chinese operatives and covertly transported—frequently through remote terrains—into Myanmar, where the scam centers are situated,” officials said.

title: Gujarat Exposed as Epicenter of Global Scam Network: CID Uncovers Billion-Dollar Fraud Ring - The420.in

AHMEDABAD: A recent investigation by the Gujarat Police’s CID (Crime) has unveiled a sprawling network of illegal call centers across India, with Gujarat emerging as a central hub for funneling fraudulently obtained money from foreign nationals.
These operations, targeting victims in countries like the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and Germany, involve sophisticated scams and extensive hawala networks.
The investigation, detailed in a 10-page FIR, highlights the role of Gujarat’s robust angadia (courier) network in transferring illicit funds. According to the FIR, the money is routed through these traditional channels and modern methods like cryptocurrency to fund operations and launder proceeds.
Key Players and Scams
The CID has identified 22 individuals as masterminds behind the scams, including Dhaval Rajesh Vazani, who was arrested in Gandhinagar. Police recovered narcotics and crucial data from his devices, revealing the operations of multiple fake call centers both in India and abroad, including Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, and the Philippines.
The scams range from tech support fraud and healthcare scams to online shopping deceptions and lottery schemes. One notable incident cited in the FIR involved a Goa-based call center scamming a Californian victim of Rs 1.4 crore worth of gold, which was then invested in a dance bar in Mumbai.
Gujarat’s Role as a Financial Processor
The report underscores Gujarat’s pivotal role as a collection hub for fraud money, owing to its extensive *angadia* network. Firms like NR Angadia, NK Angadia, and Prime Angadia are mentioned as conduits for moving illicit funds. The FIR also reveals that these funds are being funneled into real estate, jewelry businesses, and high-end establishments like clubs and dance bars in cities such as Mumbai, Goa, and Chandigarh.
Organized Crime with a Global Reach
The accused have reportedly shielded themselves from law enforcement by designating employees as owners of the call centers during police raids. The CID’s analysis indicates that these operations are highly organized, with connections spanning multiple states, including Maharashtra, Punjab, Karnataka, and Kerala, as well as international locations.
Alarming Statistics
The FIR cites data from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) in the US, which reported over 2.6 million fraud complaints linked to call centers in 2023, amounting to a staggering loss of Rs 84,860 crore.
Names Under Scrutiny
The FIR lists prominent accused individuals, including Lakhvinder Singh Gill, Narendra Gujar alias Nehru, Hardik Bharat Patel, and Meghrajsinh Gohil alias Banna, among others, all hailing from Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar districts.
This revelation has put a spotlight on the need for stricter regulations and cross-border cooperation to dismantle these fraudulent networks. The CID continues its investigation, aiming to bring the perpetrators to justice and curb the proliferation of such scams.

15% of cyber frauds involve romance scams
In 2024, India recorded over 11.21 lakh cybercrime cases. Formation of Joint Cyber Coordination teams
To combat cybercrime, seven joint cyber coordination teams have been established. These teams operate in Ahmedabad (Gujarat), Mewat, Jamtara, Hyderabad, Chandigarh, Visakhapatnam, and Guwahati. These areas are considered cybercrime hotspots. The teams work to resolve multi-jurisdictional legal conflicts and strengthen inter-state cooperation.
In Gujarat, cybercrime gangs from regions like Mewat, Jamtara, and Rajasthan engage in e-frauds. The coordination teams work closely with the central government and other states to apprehend cybercriminals and prevent such crimes. Additionally, over 1,00,000 police officers across India, including Gujarat, have received training in cybercrime investigation, forensics, and prosecution.
International reach of cybercrime
Notably, during organised efforts to combat cybercrime in Gujarat and across the country, funds obtained through fraud are often sent abroad using rented local bank accounts.
